gloss_terse: Wailing, lamentation; a mournful dirge or mourning song, especially in prophetic contexts of divine judgment.
gloss_readable: A noun denoting a loud, mournful cry or mourning song, closely associated with prophetic announcements of divine judgment. In Jeremiah 9:10-20, it appears alongside tears (dim'ah) and funeral dirges (qinah), painting a vivid picture of communal grief. Amos 5:16 speaks of professional mourners 'skilled in lamentation' (yod'e nehi), revealing an ancient Near Eastern institution of trained wailing. The Spanish 'endecha' and French 'lamentation' both capture the formalized, ritualized quality of this grief, distinguishing it from spontaneous weeping.

senses.1: A formalized wailing or lamentation, typically raised in response to prophetic judgment or catastrophic loss. In Jer 9:10 it is 'lifted up' (nasa') over the mountains, paired with weeping (bekhi) and the funeral dirge (qinah). Amos 5:16 references professional mourners who are 'skilled in nehi,' indicating this was not merely spontaneous grief but a structured vocal art. Micah 2:4 uses it as a cognate accusative, intensifying the act of lamenting. Ezekiel 2:10 lists it alongside mourning ('evel) and moaning (misped) on the prophetic scroll.

gloss_terse: Quietness, rest, tranquility; a state of peaceful calm or satisfying repose, contrasted with toil and agitation.
gloss_readable: A feminine noun conveying a deep sense of quietness, rest, or settled tranquility. Isaiah 30:15 pairs it with hashqet ('stillness'), declaring that in quietness and trust lies Israel's strength -- a powerful theological statement about restful dependence on God. Ecclesiastes uses it as the opposite of restless toil: 'a handful of quietness' outweighs 'two fistfuls of labor' (4:6). In Proverbs 29:9, it contrasts with raging and laughing, suggesting composure in the face of folly. The Spanish 'quietud' and French 'repos' both reflect its contemplative, settled quality.

senses.1: A state of quietness, rest, or peaceful tranquility, often set in deliberate contrast to agitation, toil, or foolish striving. In Isa 30:15 nachat is paired with hashqet as the twin pillars of Israel's salvation -- quiet trust rather than frantic alliance-seeking. Ecclesiastes 4:6 famously contrasts a 'palm-full of rest' with two handfuls of labor and chasing wind. Proverbs 29:9 uses it as the opposite of ragaz ('raging'), and Eccl 9:17 affirms that wise words spoken 'in quietness' are heard above a ruler's shouting. Job 36:16 extends the image to the comfort and abundance of a table 'full of fatness.'

gloss_terse: Noph (Memphis); the ancient Egyptian capital on the Nile, frequently named in prophetic oracles against Egypt.
gloss_readable: The Hebrew name for Memphis, Egypt's ancient capital situated just south of the Nile Delta. Appearing in two variant forms -- Noph and Moph -- it figures prominently in prophetic denunciations of Egypt. Jeremiah 2:16 warns that 'the sons of Noph' have broken Israel's crown, while Jeremiah 44:1 and 46:14,19 address Jewish refugees who settled there. Isaiah 19:13 declares its princes deceived, and Ezekiel 30:13 pronounces that God will destroy its idols. The Greek Septuagint renders it Memphis, preserving the Egyptian Mn-nfr ('enduring beauty').

senses.1: The proper name of the ancient Egyptian city Memphis (Egyptian Mn-nfr, 'enduring beauty'), located south of the Nile Delta near modern Cairo. It served as Egypt's political and religious capital. In prophetic literature, it represents Egyptian power and false security: Hosea 9:6 warns that 'Moph shall bury them,' Isaiah 19:13 declares its princes deluded, and Ezekiel 30:13 announces the destruction of its idols and cessation of its princes. Jeremiah uses it repeatedly (2:16; 44:1; 46:14,19) as both a symbol of Egyptian oppression and a literal destination for Judean refugees.

gloss_terse: Nergal-Sharezer; a Babylonian official present at the fall of Jerusalem, bearing a name meaning 'Nergal, protect the king.'
gloss_readable: A compound Akkadian proper name borne by a Babylonian official in Nebuchadnezzar's entourage during the siege and fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE. The name combines the Babylonian deity Nergal with the prayer element 'protect the king' (shar-usur). He appears in Jeremiah 39:3,13, where he is listed among the officials who entered Jerusalem after its walls were breached, and who later facilitated the release of Jeremiah from prison at Nebuchadnezzar's command.

senses.1: The compound proper name of a Babylonian dignitary, Nergal-Sharezer (Akkadian Nergal-shar-usur, 'O Nergal, protect the king'), who held the title Rab-mag ('chief soothsayer' or 'chief official') in the army of Nebuchadnezzar II. In Jeremiah 39:3 he is named among those who sat in the middle gate of Jerusalem after its fall, and in Jer 39:13 he participates in the delegation that retrieves Jeremiah from the court of the guard. Some scholars identify him with the later Babylonian king Neriglissar (560-556 BCE).

gloss_terse: Give, bestow, grant (Aramaic); to hand over, pay, or confer authority, used in the Biblical Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra.
gloss_readable: The Aramaic cognate of Hebrew natan, meaning 'to give, bestow, or grant.' Found exclusively in the Biblical Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra, it carries the full range of giving: divine bestowal of sovereignty (Dan 4:17,25,32 -- God 'gives' dominion to whomever He wills), requesting allowance of time (Dan 2:16), and paying tribute (Ezra 4:13; 7:20). The Spanish consistently renders it with 'dar' forms, while the French and German preserve the Aramaic morphology in their glosses, reflecting its formal, administrative register.

senses.1: To give, bestow, or grant, encompassing both human acts of giving and divine bestowal of authority. In Dan 4:17,25,32 the verb expresses God's sovereign prerogative to 'give' (yitteninnah) earthly dominion to whomever He chooses -- a key theological assertion in the Aramaic court tales. Dan 2:16 uses it for Daniel requesting that the king 'give' him time. In Ezra 4:13 it refers to paying taxes ('they will not give tribute'), and Ezra 7:20 authorizes disbursement from the royal treasury. The range spans divine sovereignty, personal petition, and fiscal administration.

gloss_terse: Twist, pervert, overthrow (Piel); to distort justice, subvert moral order, or ruin the way of the wicked.
gloss_readable: A Piel verb meaning to twist, pervert, or overturn, used in both legal and wisdom contexts. In the Torah, it describes how a bribe 'perverts' the words of the righteous (Exod 23:8; Deut 16:19), a principle so vital it is stated twice. In wisdom literature, it takes on a broader moral dimension: folly 'subverts' a person's way (Prov 19:3), wickedness 'overthrows' the sinner (Prov 13:6), and God Himself 'overturns' the plans of the treacherous (Prov 22:12). Job 12:19 extends it to the cosmic realm where God 'overthrows' even powerful leaders.

senses.1: To twist, pervert, or overturn in either a judicial or moral sense. The legal usage appears in Exod 23:8 and Deut 16:19 where a bribe 'perverts' (yesallef) the cause of the righteous -- the Spanish 'trastorna' and French 'perverts' both capture this distortion of justice. The wisdom usage in Proverbs broadens the scope: Prov 19:3 says a person's own folly 'subverts' his path; Prov 13:6 declares wickedness 'overthrows' the sinner; and Prov 22:12 affirms that the LORD 'subverts' the affairs of the treacherous. In Job 12:19 God leads priests away stripped and 'overthrows' the mighty, using the same verb for divine reversal of human power.

gloss_terse: Sepharvaim; a Mesopotamian city conquered by Assyria, whose people were resettled in Samaria after the northern exile.
gloss_readable: A proper noun in dual form designating the Mesopotamian city Sepharvaim, traditionally identified with the twin city of Sippar on the Euphrates between Baghdad and Babylon. It appears in two historical contexts: the Assyrian resettlement of foreign peoples into Samaria (2 Kgs 17:24,31), and the boasts of Assyrian envoys challenging Jerusalem's trust in God (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 36:19; 37:13). The dual ending may reflect the city's two halves -- Sippar of Shamash and Sippar of Anunitu -- on opposite sides of a canal.

senses.1: The proper name of a Mesopotamian city conquered by the Assyrian empire, appearing in dual form (Sepharvaim) possibly reflecting its two quarters: Sippar of Shamash and Sippar of Anunitu, situated on opposite sides of a canal near modern Abu Habba, Iraq. In 2 Kgs 17:24,31, its inhabitants were deported to Samaria after the fall of the northern kingdom, bringing their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech. In 2 Kgs 18:34 and Isa 36:19, the Rabshakeh cites its conquest as proof that no god can withstand Assyria, making it a test case for the theological question of divine power versus imperial might.

gloss_terse: Cake, bread-cake; a round flat bread baked on coals or hot stones, used in everyday and ritual meals.
gloss_readable: A feminine noun denoting a round, flat cake or bread-disc, typically baked directly on hot stones or coals. It appears in memorable narratives of provision and hospitality: Abraham's urgency in preparing 'ugot from fine flour for his angelic visitors (Gen 18:6), the unleavened cakes baked in haste at the Exodus (Exod 12:39), the manna ground and made into cakes (Num 11:8), and Elijah's miraculous coal-baked cake in the wilderness (1 Kgs 19:6). Hosea 7:8 uses it as a vivid metaphor: Ephraim is 'a cake not turned' -- burnt on one side, raw on the other.

senses.1: A round, flat bread-cake baked on hot stones or coals, made from various grains and used in both ordinary hospitality and sacred contexts. In Gen 18:6 Abraham instructs Sarah to make 'ugot from fine flour (solet) for the three visitors -- the Spanish 'torta' and French 'cake' both convey its flat, round shape. Exod 12:39 describes the unleavened 'ugot baked from the dough carried out of Egypt. Num 11:8 records the Israelites grinding manna and making it into cakes. In 1 Kgs 17:13 the widow of Zarephath makes a small cake for Elijah, and 1 Kgs 19:6 describes the angel's provision of a 'cake of hot stones' (ugat retsaphim). Hosea 7:8 memorably compares Ephraim to 'a cake not turned' -- half-baked and therefore ruined.

gloss_terse: Be lacking, be missing, fail (Niphal/Piel); to be absent from where one should be, always used with negation.
gloss_readable: A verb in Niphal and Piel stems meaning 'to be lacking, missing, or absent,' remarkably almost always occurring with a negative particle (lo'). This creates an emphatic affirmation of completeness: in 1 Samuel 30:19, nothing was 'missing' from what the Amalekites had taken; in 2 Samuel 17:22, not one person was lacking who had not crossed the Jordan. Isaiah 40:26 applies it cosmically -- God calls the stars by name and 'not one is missing.' Zephaniah 3:5 uses it of God Himself: morning by morning He renders justice and 'does not fail.'

senses.1: To be lacking, missing, or absent, typically negated to emphasize completeness or unfailing presence. In 1 Sam 30:19 David recovers everything and 'nothing was missing' (lo ne'dar) -- the Spanish 'faltaban' ('were missing') and French constructions preserve this sense of absence. 2 Sam 17:22 reports that by morning 'not one was lacking' who had not crossed the Jordan. Isaiah 34:16 assures that no wild creature 'is missing' from God's appointed judgment. Isaiah 40:26 applies it to the stars: God calls each by name and 'not one fails.' Isaiah 59:15 laments that truth 'has become lacking.' Zephaniah 3:5 declares that the righteous LORD 'does not fail' in administering justice. 1 Kgs 4:27 (Piel) states the governors 'let nothing be lacking.'

gloss_terse: Wares, merchandise; trade goods exchanged in commerce, used exclusively of Tyre's vast trading network in Ezekiel 27.
gloss_readable: A masculine noun found only in the plural with suffixes, meaning 'wares' or 'merchandise' -- goods left in the purchaser's hands after a transaction. It appears exclusively in Ezekiel 27, the magnificent oracle cataloguing Tyre's commercial empire. Trading partners furnished iron, tin, and lead 'as your wares' (Ezek 27:12), along with horses, mules, ivory, ebony, turquoise, coral, rubies, wheat, honey, oil, and balm. The Spanish 'productos' and French 'commerce' both reflect the mercantile context. The word may derive from 'azav ('to leave'), suggesting goods deposited or consigned in trade.

senses.1: Traded goods or merchandise, specifically items exchanged in commercial transactions, appearing only in Ezekiel 27's elaborate catalogue of Tyre's trade network. In Ezek 27:12, Tarshish traded silver, iron, tin, and lead 'as your wares' (izzevonayyik); v.14 lists horses and mules from Beth-Togarmah; v.16 mentions turquoise, purple, embroidery, and coral from Aram; v.19 records wrought iron, cassia, and calamus 'at the price of your wares'; v.22 catalogs spices and gold from Sheba and Raamah. In v.27 and v.33 the word appears in the climactic description of Tyre's fall, where all her wares sink into the heart of the seas. The etymology from 'azav ('leave, deposit') suggests goods consigned or left with a trading partner.
